question: Every year, the use of fireworks by members of the public leads to serious injuries, considerable disruption for the emergency services, damage to property, severe stress and injury to animals, not to mention a temporary but sharp spike in air pollution. More and more cities and Member States are therefore introducing (local) bans or strict restrictions.

Although Directive 2013/29/EU lays down safety requirements and categories for pyrotechnic articles (such as fireworks), the rules on sale and use by private individuals remain highly fragmented. This leads to cross-border sales and illegal trade, and undermines local or even national bans. I would like to ask the Commission the following questions in this context: 1.

Does the Commission recognise that the fragmentation of rules on the use of fireworks by private individuals undermines the effectiveness of existing bans and has negative consequences for public health, animal welfare and the environment?
Is the Commission prepared to examine the possibility of revising Directive 2013/29/EU with a view to introducing an EU-wide ban on the use and/or sale of fireworks to private individuals?

What concrete steps can the Commission take to support Member States in restricting cross-border sales to private individuals and promoting safe, professional and more environmentally friendly alternatives to fireworks?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.6.2026) The Commission is aware that many Member States have made use of the possibility provided by Directive 2013/29/EU1 to ban certain categories of pyrotechnic articles.

The Commission recognises that, while such national restrictions are intended to address safety, security or environmental risks in the Member State concerned, they can be circumvented by cross-border and online sales. The Commission has published an evaluation of Directive 2013/29/EU2 and carried out a feasibility study on reducing the security risks posed by the criminal misuse of pyrotechnics3.

Those studies show a comprehensive picture of pyrotechnics-related issues in the EU and of the functioning of the Directive. They provide a solid basis for considerations on the need of additional EU-wide measures.

Following the assessment announced in the Internal Security Strategy ProtectEU4 and to address the identified shortcomings, the Commission is currently launching the impact assessment process for a revision of the Directive on pyrotechnic articles.
